en: The Verse on the Five-Syllable Dhāraṇī.
By the Duke of Su, who held the rank of Kaifu Yitongsi, was specially promoted to the position of Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial,
received three thousand households of fiefdom, was granted purple robes, was posthumously bestowed the title of Sikong, and was conferred the posthumous name Dajian (Great Mirror).
Within hundreds of thousands of yogas, the Vajra Master has taught the noble Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta:
those who cultivate this samādhi of the five-syllable secret dharma shall swiftly enter the wisdom of all Buddhas.
One who is able to perceive the body of an accomplished Buddha with an ordinary person’s body—this dharma is most secret.
It should be received as the oral transmission of the Great Master.
One should don the armor of diligence and rely on the Dharma, not on the person.
The Dharma of the Tathāgata is non-dual, Attained by those with pure faith;
Like a universal downpour of rain, It first causes growth in fertile soil.
The secret teaching of the World-Honored One— The wise should cultivate it.
Sentient beings are narrow-minded and inferior; Deluded, they enter the suffering of the three realms of existence.
Though they hear the supreme Dharma, They do not give rise to the intent of courageous progress.
The wise give rise to compassion And seek primordial awakening for their sake.
Just as when one approaches a mountain of jewels, the wise person goes there to gather them,
while the fool knows not to go and thus suffers manifold miseries for long days;
so too, if one hears this Dharma, one immediately knows the most excellent path.
Those who abide in the great vows— such people are capable of this training.
If anyone hears this Dharma and is struck with awe, feels profound sorrow and joy,
weeps, and their hair stands on end— such people are capable of this training.
If there are those who hear this Dharma, their single-mindedness shall not be disturbed;
their faculties will be pure and serene, and such people are fit to study it.
If there are those who hear this Dharma, they will accordingly attain the flavor of the joy of dhyāna.
One who does not delight in worldly pleasures is such a person as is fit to train;
if they hear this Dharma, they do not wait for the right time or day,
nor do they seek a complete set of conditions, but advance directly with a straightforward mind.
Not experiencing the suffering of seeking when lacking ritual requisites,
and being well-versed in the Dharma-offering— such a person is fit to study and recite mantras,
tasting them like the celestial nectar of immortality.
With single-minded resolve, one must wish to hear; such a person is capable of learning.
With both hands, one forms the secret mudrā; conceiving a sense of great reverence, as if holding Mount Sumeru; such a person is capable of learning.
This Dharma was taught by all Buddhas for those of the Supreme Vehicle;
yet those of inferior faculties and natures, being filled with doubt, cannot believe in it.
Because the nature of sentient beings is pure, it is through the power of the Buddhas' original vows.
By means of the seal of the dharmas of correspondence, one manifests the bodies of all the noble ones;
even within a single sitting, one shall attain supreme perfect enlightenment.
If one follows this Dharma, one should maintain such faith.
Or if, for even a single thought-moment, one says,
"I am an ordinary person," thereby slandering the Buddhas of the three times; or if, within the Dharma, one incurs a grave offense,
has not received the stage of empowerment, or is not a fellow practitioner.
One should not speak falsely; like one who guards a jewel within their topknot,
as the sūtras describe the locations— whether in an araṇya,
by a river, a pond, or the seashore, or on the pure peaks of famous mountains.
Having attained the Way and turned the wheel of Dharma, the Sage established his seat of accomplishment;
he selected the ground to build a vihāra, following the requirements of the site,
leveling and purifying the earth with fine materials, and scattering various seasonal flowers.
Assisting the Dharma through various vows of discipline, as taught by the various schools,
one bathes the body until it is pure, puts on exquisite garments,
and adorns oneself with fragrant ointments; then, one proceeds to the gateway of the vihāra.
First, visualize one's own body as Vajrasattva, holding a vajra in the left hand and grasping a luminous bell in the right.
At the gateway, recite the syllable HŪṂ; with wrathful eyes, dispel all inauspiciousness.

Then, prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground, one reverently bows at the feet of the World-Honored One and takes refuge with a single mind, forming the thought that the Buddha dwells eternally.
Next, kneeling with both knees on the ground, one confesses and reveals all transgressions.
With these words of purity, Repent with sincere devotion.
One should silently recite this once, Uttering the syllable *A* aloud:
"The immeasurable sins accumulated Are purified, leaving none behind."
Next, with a mind of reverent supplication, form the Vajrotthāna mudrā and silently recite this secret mantra to summon the Buddhas of the ten directions:
With both hands in vajra fists, hook the thumbs and wisdom fingers together.
The peaks of the advancing power join together; facing the heart, perform three upward beckoning gestures.
One will then know that all Tathāgatas have arisen from samādhi.
One should observe within the void space all the Buddhas and the assembly of sages.
Pervading the ocean of the Dharma-realm, Without any gaps or omissions,
through the power of their vows, They all descend to the site of enlightenment;
Binding the vajra mudrā and visualizing, One pays homage at the feet of all Buddhas.
The two hands are turned away from each other; visualizing the *tathāgatas* with the *vajra-aṅkuśa* (hook) of the *dāna* and *prajñā* hands, one pays homage.
Kneeling long on the ground, the methods for scattering [flowers] upon the crown of the head are of four kinds;
these should be performed in sequence according to the specific rite.
With body upright and limbs fixed in meditative posture, seated cross-legged upon a pure lunar disc,
one should then take the syllable Maṭha; with the two eyes as the sun and moon,
emitting vajra-flames, one gazes upon all the Tathāgatas.
Next, looking back toward all directions, one burns away the hearts, tongues, and both hands of those who create obstacles;
the syllable HŪṂ radiates golden light like that of all the Tathāgatas,
appearing as the sublime form of the teaching of the Dharma.
Next, facing the Buddhas of the ten directions, bind the seal of the great vow:
with the vajra-bind of the ten perfections, erect the two peaks of the patience and wish fingers to indicate the Buddhas and all the sages, and pray that they remember their former vows.
Next, bind the mudrā of joy and offer this samaya-pleasure:
interlace the fingers of the ten fingers externally; join the *kṣānti* and *praṇidhi* fingers together at the center;
and join the *dāna*, *prajñā*, *dhyāna*, and *jñāna* fingers respectively, holding them upright.
Visualize upon the two breasts: on the right is *tra* and on the left is *ṭa*, like the panels of a palace door.
Reciting these secret syllables, one should then use the vajra-hand to pull them open three times.
Visualize an eight-petaled lotus in front;
with the two hands in the vajra-bond (*vajrabandha*) mudrā, place the thumbs (*dhyāna-jñāna*) within it.
Reciting this secret mantra, the syllable *A* enters the palace, its color that of white light.
As before, with the *A* syllable mudrā, extend the left index finger and bend it to support [the thumb], thereby closing the gate of the heart;
by means of the *Jñāna* syllable, one attains firmness.
Next, bind the Trailokyavijaya mudrā and abide in the samādhi of wrath.
One who wishes to perform this rite should first abide in a mind of great compassion.
With both hands in the vajra-fist mudrā, hook the thumbs and wisdom fingers (tarjanī) with their tips facing outward,
extend the index fingers (vajra-vaśitā), and remain in the posture of the *hiḥ*-chant.
Frowning with a smile yet full of wrath, the four *hūṃ*s sound like the roar of thunder.
Visualize the Secret Keeper (*Guhyapada*) and his retinue; receiving the command, they stand in attendance.
Moving counter-clockwise performs the expulsion (*vidhūnana*); moving clockwise performs the boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*).
Next, bind the Samādhi-mudrā: The practitioner, abiding in samādhi, interlaces the two hands with the backs facing outward;
sitting upright in the full lotus posture, with the mouth and teeth closed, they count the breaths to bring the mind to stillness.
The Tathāgatas previously invited, who fill the entire expanse of space,
snapped their fingers to awaken me, causing me to contemplate the gateway of the letter A;
silently reciting this secret mantra, I received their instruction and stood in attendance.
When reciting this silently once, one should imagine it as a lunar disc for the sake of further purification; then,
while reciting these secret words upon the pure lunar disc, one visualizes the seed-syllable *daṃ*.
To accomplish the vajra-sword, one should recite these secret words over a pure moon disc; its sharpness shall pierce through to the light,
gradually becoming all-pervasive until its extent is equal to space.
Nor does one see one's own body or any other signs;
next, one should gradually visualize the sword. Reciting these words of withdrawal, all the Tathāgatas of space are gathered in along with the sword.
Having made [the image] equal in size to one's own body, it then becomes the form of the Original Sage;
its body color is like purple-gold, appearing in the likeness of a wondrous youth with five topknots adorning his head and wearing a precious crown of the five directions.
In his right hand he holds a vajra-sword from which flames of fire issue upward;
in his left hand he holds a blue lotus bearing the Prajñā-pāramitā scripture.
He abides amidst various exquisite colors and forms, his body situated within a pure moon disc.
Once the practitioner has established themselves herein, they should reflect as follows:
"I now firmly abide in the body of the vajra-sword, the body of the mahāsamaya."
All Tathāgatas of the three times manifestly attain equal and perfect enlightenment.
Abiding in this samādhi, I take the vajra-sword as my body;
having formed this thought, I recite the secret mantra as follows:
One should bind the original sacred mudrā: for the empowerment of the samādhi-form, interlace the two hands with the palms facing outward;
extend both the *kṣānti* (ring) and *praṇidhāna* (little finger) fingers straight, then bend the second joints upward so that they resemble the peak of a sword.
At the heart, forehead, throat, and crown, recite this once at each location.
Then, bind the five-crested mudrā, thereby becoming fully endowed with the perfections of ethical discipline,
wisdom, generosity, diligence, meditative concentration, and the power of primordial awareness.
The mudrās for the Patience and Vow [perfections] and so forth are all combined;

their form is like the Five-Peaked Mudrā, placed at the heart, both shoulders, and the throat, with the last placed upon the crown of the head—this is called the Five-Tufted Mudrā. Recite this root mantra.
Next, form the initiation mudrā: join the palms of both hands, with the thumbs and index fingers entering within;
place the middle and ring fingers in the shape of a maṇi jewel at the forehead while reciting the secret mantra, visualizing the Buddhas pouring water upon the crown of my head.
Next, bind the Jewel Garland mudrā: release the previous mudrā and separate it into the positions of the forehead and the back of the crown;
with the mudrā, perform three circumambulations starting from the wisdom side of the mandala, in the manner of a trailing garland.
Next, don the firm armor: with the two hands in vajra-fists, extend the fingers of the right hand forward.
Recite "Oṃ," visualizing the surface of the fingers as green light that flows without ceasing, like drawing out lotus fibers.
From the heart, back, navel, and waist, To the two knees and the area behind the seat;
Gradually reaching the throat and neck, Then the forehead and the crown of the head;
Subsequently, exerting effort, perform three circumambulations each, Beginning from the front of the altar and dispersing with wisdom.
With two hands hanging down, draped in celestial robes—this is called the Armor of Compassion.
Next, visualize the heart of the painted image; contemplate the syllable *Dāṃ* as a sword, which then returns to the form of the original deity, just as was visualized previously.

One should then invite [the deity] with the Hook Mudrā: join the two hands into vajra-fists, hook the thumb and ring finger of the wisdom-hand (tarjanī) behind the other, extend the middle fingers, and beckon with them bent.
Next, enter with the Noose Mudrā; the form of this mudrā is identical to the previous one.
Using only the power of the thumbs, they support one another like the shape of a ring;
next, one stops with the seal of the chain. With both hands in vajra-fists, the power of the thumbs acts like a hook and a chain; by this, one is able to bring [the winds] to rest.
Next, one should rejoice with the ghaṇṭā-mudrā;
then, with the same mudrās as before, one should join the fingers of the dhyāna, prajñā, and vīrya-pāramitās, hooking them together in reverse order.
Thereafter, one should offer arghya water, filling a sublime vessel with fragrant water.
Place exquisite flowers together and, holding them up to the forehead, offer them;
next, perform the four inner offerings.
The Mahārati goddesses emanated by the Honored One Samantaprabha present delight to all the Noble Ones.
Form the two-vajra-bond with the thumbs and wisdom-fingers extended side by side;
visualize clouds of exquisite celestial maidens filling the lands of the ten directions.
Next, offer the garland mudrā, extending the arms and holding them forward.
Visualize clouds of wondrous jewel garlands filling the entire realm of space.
Next, form the mudrā of song and offer worship with it.
From the previous mudrā at the navel, gradually move it upward to the mouth and release it.
Visualizing the voice of a kinnara, one makes offerings to the assembly of noble ones.

Next, one performs the offering of dance; with both hands in the vajra-fist mudrā, one offers to the noble ones of the ten directions by circling to the right and scattering [the flowers] above the crown of the head.
Visualize clouds of exquisite music and dance pervading all worlds;
next, with the incense mudrā, universally perfume all worlds.
With the vajra-bond mudrā released downward, clouds of fragrance pervade the entire dharma-realm.
Next, with the Flower-Sprinkling Mudrā, adorn all worlds;
from the upper part of the Vajra-bond, scatter flowers so that a flower-net pervades the void.
Next, offer the Wisdom-Lamp Mudrā, universally illuminating all darkness.
The preceding signs of dhyāna and prajñā press together; next, this light of wisdom universally radiates.
Then offer the mudrā of incense: with the posture of applying incense to the chest, through clouds of liberating fragrance, purify the realms of all sentient beings.
Having completed the inner and outer offerings,
one should then sequentially and mindfully form the fundamental secret mudrā.
Recite the hundred-syllable mantra without releasing the fundamental mudrā, and then recite the previously contemplated vidyā-mantra.
There are four ways of recollecting the Dharma: First, *samādhi*, which means visualizing the clarity of that which is recollected.
From the mouth of the *iṣṭadevatā* (meditational deity), light rays stream forth;
following these rays, they enter one’s own mouth, circumambulate to the right, and spread across the moon-disc of the heart.
Just as when a crystal bead is placed upon a bright mirror, "A" signifies non-arising;
"Ra" signifies freedom from the stain of dust;
"Pa" signifies the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); and all phenomena are equal in their nature.
This refers to the meaning of the absence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
"Namo" refers to the meaning of the absence of intrinsic nature and characteristics. Although these five phrases differ, their nature is non-dual.
For one whose mind is united with this nature, there is no need for further discrimination.
The Buddha praised that which is beyond thought; it is neither thought nor non-thought.
When thought and non-thought have both ceased, even up to the *dhāraṇī*—such is the meaning of these four lines, expounded in accordance with the *sūtras*.

Second is the recitation of vocal sounds (*vāk-patha-smṛti*): relying on the previous visualization of the syllables, one remains free from variations in pitch, height, or speed, with the force of the sound like the ringing of a bell.
Third is the adamantine recitation (*vajra-smṛti*): relying on the previous visualization, one enters into the syllables.
Closely joining the lips and teeth, move the tongue slightly;
fourth is the visualization for subduing māras:
taking compassion as the foundation, manifest a wrathful exterior with knitted brows and a forceful voice.
Although there are four types of distinctions, they are non-dual within a single moment.
With two hands holding a rosary— either a bodhi seed or a lotus seed—
one should employ the lotus mudrā, or abide in the mudrā of preaching the Dharma.
Morning, noon, dusk, and midnight—these four times are the fixed standard.
This method is the foremost; it is the most secret of secrets.
One should disregard even body and life, relying single-mindedly upon the definitive meaning.
A practitioner who follows the principle and dwells in meditative concentration should contemplate this Dharma,
in order to give rise to the function of samādhi and swiftly attain omniscience; [this is for those of] inferior faculties.
For those whose delusion and craving are in disarray, one should likewise exhort them to practice this dharma in order to eliminate the veil of afflictions and enter the wisdom of tranquility;
once the prescribed number of recitations is completed, one should again offer argha water.
With a joyful mind, one should recite praises with sublime tones;
furthermore, one should present the eight offerings while feeling deep longing and devotion.
Then, having bound the fundamental secret mudrā, one disperses it from the heart and the crown of the head.
One perceives the Honored One in the midst of space; Furthermore, one returns to one's own palace.
For those who abide in this samādhi, there is none more supreme or unsurpassed— Except for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—for whom no other person is worthy of love or veneration.
Desiring to accord with the world, one should manifest acts of reverence;
one should contemplate the head of that person as possessing the marks of a Buddha or Bodhisattva.
Reciting the hundred-syllable mantra is the secret within the Dharma.
If the mind should become distracted, one should silently recite [the mantra].
As for the essential points previously received orally from the Great Master,
they cannot be described by the power of a fool, being like a single drop of water in the ocean.
Fearing that I might offend the Great Sage,
I am filled with trepidation and trembling like a lowly fool; yet, though I offer but a small measure of ambrosia,
do not let it be rendered ineffective by treating me with contempt.
Though I may take the form of a jackal or a rākṣasa, for the sake of the Dharma I shall accept such states.
May I, by this merit, universally awaken all sentient beings;
having myself escaped the net of worldly existence, may I practice according to what I have taught.
The Verse on the Five-Syllable Dhāraṇī
